threats.title: Reused passwords let attackers sign in as API client
threats.description: API client authenticates over the public internet. Attackers try passwords leaked from other services against it, and anyone who reuses a password is exposed even though nothing in this system was breached.

threats.title: Stolen credentials let an attacker act as API client
threats.description: API client proves who it is with a credential such as a password, key or token. If that credential is stolen, leaked or guessed, the attacker is indistinguishable from the real entity until someone notices.
threats.status_reason: An /api/login token is a bearer: whoever holds it acts as the account until it expires, and it is not revoked by sign out everywhere (pinned by apps/api/test/contract/session-tokens.test.ts, 'is not revoked by sign out everywhere')

threats.title: API client can deny having done something
threats.description: If the system keeps no trustworthy record of what API client asked for, the entity can later claim it never did, and the system cannot show otherwise. That matters most for orders, approvals, deletions and payments.
threats.status_reason: An account's writes are logged with its account id, but the log is stdout, not persisted or tamper-evident, so a person can deny a change; the persisted audit log of Phase 6 closes it (tracked as the open threats of Threat model API)

threats.title: Stolen credentials let an attacker act as LLM provider (hosted)
threats.description: LLM provider (hosted) proves who it is with a credential such as a password, key or token. If that credential is stolen, leaked or guessed, the attacker is indistinguishable from the real entity until someone notices.
threats.status_reason: The provider proves who it is with its TLS certificate, which Scrylux checks because a hosted provider must be reached over https; the provider's keys and certificates are the provider's to protect, outside Scrylux. An impostor's answers are still checked against their schema and never executed.

threats.title: LLM provider (hosted) can deny having done something
threats.description: If the system keeps no trustworthy record of what LLM provider (hosted) asked for, the entity can later claim it never did, and the system cannot show otherwise. That matters most for orders, approvals, deletions and payments.
threats.status_reason: The provider asks Scrylux for nothing and only answers requests; it keeps its own usage and billing record per key, outside Scrylux. Scrylux logs one line per request with the provider, model, outcome, tokens and cost, but no content (packages/llm/src/log.ts).

threats.title: Anyone inside the network can pose as Operator
threats.description:
Operator connects from inside the network and does not prove who it is. A compromised machine or a curious colleague on the same network can send the same requests and be taken for the real entity.
A private network is not an identity check.
threats.status_reason: The operator acts on the host, not through a network interface of Scrylux, so there is nothing for someone in the network to pose against

threats.title: Actions by Operator cannot be tied to anyone
threats.description: Operator does not authenticate, so the system cannot say who was behind a request. After an incident or a dispute there is nothing to link the actions to a person or a system.
threats.status_reason: The operator acts on the host and its environment, not through Scrylux; the host's own audit (in the AWS guide, Systems Manager Session Manager, deployment.md) is the record

threats.title: Operator can deny having done something
threats.description: If the system keeps no trustworthy record of what Operator asked for, the entity can later claim it never did, and the system cannot show otherwise. That matters most for orders, approvals, deletions and payments.
threats.status_reason: What the operator does on the host is outside Scrylux; the host's own audit (in the AWS guide, Systems Manager Session Manager) is the record

threats.description: Secrets manager proves who it is with a credential such as a password, key or token. If that credential is stolen, leaked or guessed, the attacker is indistinguishable from the real entity until someone notices.
threats.status_reason: Access to the secret is by the instance's role, limited to that one secret (deployment.md, step4); the credentials of that role are the provider's to protect, outside Scrylux

threats.title: Secrets manager can deny having done something

threats.title: A stolen session lets an attacker act as a signed-in user of Accounts API
threats.description: Once a user has signed in, Accounts API recognises them by a session credential. Anyone who obtains that credential, for example through a script injected into a page, a leaked log line or a stolen device, can act as the user until the session ends.

threats.title: Another program can pose as Accounts API to the components that call it
threats.description: Components that call Accounts API need to be sure they are talking to the real one. If an attacker can take over its name or address, or sit on the path to it, they can answer in its place and collect what callers send.
threats.status_reason: Accounts API is code inside the API's own process, not a separate service, so there is no network call to impersonate

threats.title: Crafted input from the internet can change what Accounts API does
threats.description: Accounts API takes input from the public internet. Anyone can send it data shaped to be misread: an oversized value, a wrong type, or text that looks like a command or query. If the process trusts that input, the attacker decides what it does.

threats.title: The code, dependencies or configuration of Accounts API can be altered
threats.description: An attacker who can change what Accounts API runs gets everything the process can do. The route can be a poisoned dependency, a tampered build or image, or a changed configuration or environment variable.

threats.title: Access to sensitive data through Accounts API leaves no trail
threats.description: Accounts API handles sensitive data. If reads, exports and changes of that data are not recorded with who did them, a leak or a misuse cannot be traced, and a person who misused their access can deny it.
threats.status_reason: The operation reads nothing: it only creates an account; its own missing log is the open threat of Accounts API

threats.title: Actions taken through Accounts API cannot be reconstructed later
threats.description: Without a record of security-relevant events, nobody can say afterwards who signed in, who changed what or what an attacker did. Accounts API may do the right thing and still be unable to prove it.

threats.title: A signed-in user may read someone else's data through Accounts API
threats.description: Accounts API knows who the caller is, but knowing who someone is does not say which records they may see. If it hands back whatever record is asked for, a signed-in user can read other people's data by changing an identifier in a request.
threats.status_reason: Accounts API has no read operation: its one operation creates an account and answers the new account's id and name (apps/api/src/routes/users.ts)

threats.title: Accounts API may reveal its internals in error messages
threats.description: Detailed errors help developers and attackers alike. Stack traces, query text, file paths and version numbers in a response show an attacker how Accounts API is built and where to push.

threats.title: Accounts API may write sensitive data into logs, metrics or traces
threats.description: Logs are copied, indexed, shipped and read by many people and tools. If Accounts API writes sensitive values into them, such as passwords, tokens, personal data or request bodies, the data ends up in places with much weaker protection than the system it came from.

threats.title: Accounts API stops working when something it depends on fails
threats.description: Accounts API relies on other components such as databases, queues and other services. If one of them is slow or down and the process waits for it without a limit, requests pile up and the failure spreads.
threats.status_reason: Scrylux has one PostgreSQL and no failover: when it is down every operation but /health fails, and nothing is written half-done (generation, import and writes are one transaction each). Availability of the database is the operator's

threats.title: Anyone on the internet can overwhelm Accounts API
threats.description: Accounts API accepts work from the public internet. Without limits, a flood of requests, a few very expensive ones or a slow connection held open on purpose can use up its CPU, memory or connections and shut out real users.

threats.title: A script injected into the page creates accounts
threats.description: An attacker's script running in the signed-in web app could try to use the page's access token to create an account.

threats.title: A signed-in user can reach functions in Accounts API that are meant for others
threats.description: Accounts API requires callers to sign in, but being signed in is not the same as being allowed. If it does not check permissions for each function, an ordinary user may reach administrative or other users' functions by calling them directly.

threats.title: Input from the internet could make Accounts API run an attacker's code
threats.description: Accounts API is reachable from the internet. If it evaluates input as code, deserializes untrusted data, handles uploaded files unsafely or uses a vulnerable dependency, an attacker can make it run their code and gain whatever the process itself can do.

threats.title: A file claims rule-generated provenance for a threat
threats.description: A Scrylux file, or an OTM file carrying Scrylux's mark, can say that a threat is rule-generated, with any rule reference. Scrylux cannot check it, and a later "Generate threats" then treats that threat as its own.

threats.status_reason: The replay gets one 5-minute access token and no new credential, and is only possible for 30 seconds after a renewal (apps/api/src/session/store.ts, GRACE_SECONDS; pinned by apps/api/test/contract/session.test.ts, 'treats the replaced credential inside the grace window as a grace hit: 200 and no Set-Cookie'). Replay after the window ends the session.

threats.title: Another program can pose as Sign-in and sessions to the components that call it
threats.description: Components that call Sign-in and sessions need to be sure they are talking to the real one. If an attacker can take over its name or address, or sit on the path to it, they can answer in its place and collect what callers send.
threats.status_reason: Sign-in and sessions is code inside the API's own process, not a separate service, so there is no network call to impersonate

threats.title: Anyone on the internet can call Sign-in and sessions without proving who they are
threats.description: Sign-in and sessions accepts connections from the public internet and does not require callers to authenticate. It cannot tell one caller from another, so it cannot limit what any of them may do, and every caller is effectively anonymous and equally trusted.

threats.title: Password guessing spread across many addresses is slowed but not stopped
threats.description: Failed sign-ins are counted per username-and-address and per address, so an attacker who spreads guesses over many addresses, or many IPv6 /64 ranges, is slowed per address and not stopped.
threats.status_reason: Slowed per address, not stopped: guessing spread across many addresses or /64s is never counted together. The throttle deliberately has no per-account lockout, so an attacker cannot lock the admin out. General rate limiting is planned for Phase 6 (plan.md).

threats.title: Crafted input from the internet can change what Sign-in and sessions does
threats.description: Sign-in and sessions takes input from the public internet. Anyone can send it data shaped to be misread: an oversized value, a wrong type, or text that looks like a command or query. If the process trusts that input, the attacker decides what it does.

threats.title: The code, dependencies or configuration of Sign-in and sessions can be altered
threats.description: An attacker who can change what Sign-in and sessions runs gets everything the process can do. The route can be a poisoned dependency, a tampered build or image, or a changed configuration or environment variable.

threats.title: Access to sensitive data through Sign-in and sessions leaves no trail
threats.description: Sign-in and sessions handles sensitive data. If reads, exports and changes of that data are not recorded with who did them, a leak or a misuse cannot be traced, and a person who misused their access can deny it.

threats.title: Actions taken through Sign-in and sessions cannot be reconstructed later
threats.description: Without a record of security-relevant events, nobody can say afterwards who signed in, who changed what or what an attacker did. Sign-in and sessions may do the right thing and still be unable to prove it.

threats.title: Sensitive data handled by Sign-in and sessions is open to anyone who can reach it
threats.description: Sign-in and sessions handles sensitive data and does not require callers to authenticate. Anyone who can connect can ask for the data, with nothing to tie the request to a person who is allowed to see it.

threats.title: Sign-in and sessions may reveal its internals in error messages
threats.description: Detailed errors help developers and attackers alike. Stack traces, query text, file paths and version numbers in a response show an attacker how Sign-in and sessions is built and where to push.

threats.title: Sign-in and sessions may write sensitive data into logs, metrics or traces
threats.description: Logs are copied, indexed, shipped and read by many people and tools. If Sign-in and sessions writes sensitive values into them, such as passwords, tokens, personal data or request bodies, the data ends up in places with much weaker protection than the system it came from.

threats.title: Anyone on the internet can overwhelm Sign-in and sessions
threats.description: Sign-in and sessions accepts work from the public internet. Without limits, a flood of requests, a few very expensive ones or a slow connection held open on purpose can use up its CPU, memory or connections and shut out real users.

threats.title: Sign-in and sessions stops working when something it depends on fails
threats.description: Sign-in and sessions relies on other components such as databases, queues and other services. If one of them is slow or down and the process waits for it without a limit, requests pile up and the failure spreads.
threats.status_reason: Scrylux has one PostgreSQL and no failover: when it is down every operation but /health fails, and nothing is written half-done (generation, import and writes are one transaction each). Availability of the database is the operator's

threats.title: Input from the internet could make Sign-in and sessions run an attacker's code
threats.description: Sign-in and sessions is reachable from the internet. If it evaluates input as code, deserializes untrusted data, handles uploaded files unsafely or uses a vulnerable dependency, an attacker can make it run their code and gain whatever the process itself can do.

threats.title: Changes to Account and session records cannot be traced to whoever made them

threats.title: Reads of sensitive data in Account and session records leave no record
threats.description: Account and session records stores sensitive data. If reads are not logged, a leak cannot be traced to an account or a time, and anyone with access can look without being accountable.

threats.description: Sensitive data in Account and session records does not stay in one place: it is copied into backups, exports, replicas and test environments. Each copy is often guarded less well than the store itself, and any one of them can leak the lot.
threats.status_reason: Scrylux makes no backups: a copy is the operator's database backup or snapshot, which has the protection the operator gives it (the AWS guide's RDS storage is encrypted by default, step5-rds-guide.md). The copies Scrylux does make, a report and an export, are made on purpose and are accepted as threats of Report builder and Import and export

threats.title: Sensitive data in Account and session records can be read from disks, snapshots or stolen media
threats.description: Account and session records stores sensitive data without encryption at rest. Anyone who gets hold of the underlying disk, a snapshot, a backup file or a decommissioned drive can read it directly, bypassing every access control in the application.
threats.status_reason: Scrylux does not encrypt at rest: that is the storage's job. The AWS guide's RDS has encryption on by default (step5-rds-guide.md); the compose volume has none, and the compose defaults are for local use. Credentials are protected separately, as bcrypt hashes and SHA-256 digests

threats.title: Too many people or services can read sensitive data in Account and session records

threats.description: Worker settings carries data from Operator to Worker without encryption, and the connection leaves one trust zone for another. Anyone on the network path between the zones can read it.
threats.status_reason: The operator places the settings in the host's environment (a systemd unit, a compose file or a secrets manager); Scrylux defines no network path for them

threats.title: Operator can flood Worker with messages across a trust boundary
threats.description: Worker settings crosses a trust boundary. The sending side is less trusted than the receiving side, so it can send more than Worker can handle, by mistake or on purpose, and crowd out other work.
threats.status_reason: The operator sets the environment once; there is no stream to flood

threats.title: A look-alike image or registry is mistaken for the project's
threats.description: Someone could publish an image with a similar name, or a user could pull from the wrong registry.
threats.status_reason: Every release's notes name the exact image and its digest, and a user can be told no more than that without a signature. Accepted until Phase 6 (Verifiable release images, plan.md).

threats.title: A version tag is forged by someone who is not a maintainer
threats.description: The release pipeline starts on the push of a v* tag. A tag made by anyone else, or on the wrong commit, would try to publish a release.

threats.title: A build or release step is replaced with a malicious one
threats.description: The release pipeline builds and publishes the image users run. A changed action, a changed BuildKit image or a changed step would put code into it.

threats.title: A hostile or misconfigured model endpoint answers with crafted output
threats.description: An LLM provider, or an endpoint the operator points Scrylux at by mistake, could answer with output shaped to make Scrylux store or act on something it should not.

threats.title: A job is run twice, by a worker that was only slow and the one that took it over
threats.description: A worker holds a job on a lease it renews. If it is slow rather than gone, another worker can take the job over, and the first could still write its progress or its result afterwards.

threats.title: A published image is replaced after publication
threats.description: The registry does not enforce immutable tags, so whoever has write access to the package could push a different image under a published version.

threats.title: Tampering with third-party actions and images in the pipeline
threats.description: The build and release pipeline runs third-party GitHub Actions and pulls base and service images from outside the repository; a changed action or image would change what is built and tested.

threats.title: The test job downloads browser binaries and system packages from outside the repository
threats.description: The required test job installs Playwright's browser binaries and system packages from the network.
threats.status_reason: They are pinned only by the lockfile's @playwright/test version, which Dependabot's cooldown and pnpm's minimumReleaseAge cover (docs/ci.md). Accepted in Phase 1 Milestone 6, when the browser tests became part of the required check.

threats.title: pnpm does not verify its own version
threats.description: pnpm-workspace.yaml sets pmOnFail: ignore, so pnpm no longer checks the running pnpm against packageManager.
threats.status_reason: It keeps pnpm-lock.yaml a single YAML document, which GitHub's dependency graph needs to read it (dependabot-core#15904); without it Dependabot alerts are silently off. CI and the Docker build install the exact pnpm version through Corepack, which compensates. To be reverted when #15904 ships (pnpm-workspace.yaml).

threats.title: A user cannot tell who built an image or from which commit
threats.description: Without a signature or an attestation, a user can compare an image's digest and read its labels, but cannot prove who produced it.

threats.title: A pipeline job leaks a repository secret, for instance to a fork
threats.description: A workflow that read a repository secret, or ran fork code with write access, could expose it.

threats.title: A provider key kept in the shared secret reaches the API process
threats.description: The worker is the only process that uses a provider key, but both processes read the secrets-manager secret for the database credentials, so a key stored there is readable by the API process too, which never uses it.
threats.status_reason: The compose files and the documentation give the keys to the worker alone, in its environment (docker-compose.yml, docs/install.md, Which process gets what); an operator who keeps keys in the shared secret has chosen to share them with the app. A separate secret for the worker would close the gap and is not scheduled

threats.title: A secret reaches the image, a release asset or the pipeline's log
threats.description: An image, an attached file or a log line that held a credential would publish it with the release.

threats.title: A job never ends, or is held by a worker that is gone
threats.description: A worker can stop in the middle of a job, a provider can hold a request open, and a job can keep failing and running again.

threats.title: Many accounts can start provider checks one after another and spend on the provider
threats.description: Every job is capped and every account is limited, but any signed-in account can create more accounts, each with its own cooldown, and the caps bound one job and not spend over time. A request that a crashed worker was making may also be uncounted, though the provider may bill it.

threats.title: A tag push runs the release workflow as defined at the tagged commit
threats.description: Whatever the release workflow says at the commit that is tagged is what runs with the write permissions, so the gate cannot guard against a commit whose gate was edited.
threats.status_reason: Whoever can create a version tag can already change the workflow and the rulesets, so the tag adds no power the repository owner lacks, and the owner is the only one who can create it. Accepted until Phase 6 gives the project roles and organisation-level required workflows.

threats.title: An install is left running on the documented default credentials
threats.description: The quickstart's compose file starts with admin / admin, a development signing secret and a default database password. Someone who exposes it without changing them gives anyone the keys.

threats.title: An over-privileged pipeline token, or an admin who can bypass the checks
threats.description: A write-capable default token, or a repository admin who could merge around the required checks, would let unreviewed or untested code through.

threats.title: Any signed-in account can see and cancel every job and start a provider check
threats.description: There are no roles, so a job is not private to the account that started it, and any signed-in account can make the provider spend by starting a check, where until Phase 3 Milestone 2 only an operator with a shell could.
threats.status_reason: There are no roles before Phase 6 (the open risk of the model as a whole). A provider check sends fixed text and spends little, and it is bounded by the caps, the limit on an account's active jobs and the cooldown. The widening was called out in Milestone 2's spec (FR-065) and is a justified widening in the constitution's Threat Model section

threats.title: The publishing credential is stolen or broader than needed
threats.description: The release pipeline holds a token that can write packages and releases. If it leaked, or were broader than needed, an attacker could publish as the project.
